title: This 'Moonish Thingy' Is Blurring the Line Between Planet and Moon
summary:
A newly discovered cosmic object is unlike anything seen before. It's not a planet. It's not a moon. It's a third thing we don't have a name for yet. The object, about as massive as Jupiter, orbits a brown dwarf—a "failed star" that's too big to be a planet but too small to shine as a true star. That brown dwarf, in turn, loops around a star called CD-35 2722. This is the first known system to host an "exosatellite," a term coined by researchers because no existing word fits.

"It's so different from the structure of the solar system that all the words we invented to describe the solar system just aren't really working," says Kevin Hoy, an astronomer at University Diego Portales in Chile. He and his team used the Very Large Telescope to observe the brown dwarf between 2023 and 2026. They detected periodic shifts in the wavelengths of light emitted by the brown dwarf, revealing that the gravity of a massive object was tugging it to and fro. This technique has been used to find planets around other stars, but this is the first time it has turned up what Hoy calls a "moonish thingy"—something orbiting a bigger something that's orbiting a still bigger something.

The discovery reignites an old debate about what counts as a planet. The International Astronomical Union (IAU) defined an exoplanet in 2018 as an object at most 13 times the mass of Jupiter that orbits a star, a brown dwarf, or a stellar remnant. Under that definition, a Jupiter-sized object orbiting a brown dwarf is a planet, regardless of whether the brown dwarf orbits a star. "That kind of forces the companion to be a planet," says David Kipping, an astronomer at Columbia University who studies exomoons. "We can argue about if the IAU definition is wrong or right, but by the current IAU definition, [the new object is] a planet."

But Hoy disagrees. "It doesn't feel the same as what normal planets are doing," he says. In our solar system, there's a clear hierarchy: moons orbit planets, planets orbit the sun. But this system is different. As Hoy puts it, "We'd be comfortable calling Mercury a moon if it orbited Jupiter and calling Ganymede a planet if it orbited a star." So maybe we need new words for these cosmic oddities.
why_it_matters: This discovery shows that the universe does not always fit the neat categories we learn in school. How we define planets and moons shapes what scientists look for next — and the teens following this story may one day be the ones deciding those definitions.

background_read: The Very Large Telescope (a set of huge telescopes in northern Chile run by a European partnership) made this discovery possible. A brown dwarf is sometimes called a failed star: it forms like a star but never gets hot enough to shine steadily on its own. Brown dwarfs are cooler and dimmer than stars, which makes them good targets for spotting companions by their gravitational tug. The International Astronomical Union (the global body of astronomers that also made the famous decision to reclassify Pluto as a dwarf planet) sets the official definitions for objects in space. CD-35 2722 is the ordinary star that the brown dwarf loops around. Using small shifts in light wavelengths, Kevin Hoy's team found a Jupiter-sized companion — and the result has scientists debating whether 'planet,' 'moon,' and 'satellite' still make sense.

perspectives.description: The discovery is a breakthrough because it reveals a new class of system no one had seen before. It also gives scientists a rare chance to test how planets form and migrate in strange environments, which could lead to more finds like it.

Calling the object a 'planet' just because it fits a formal definition may hide how different it really is from the planets we know. If scientific names don't describe how the object formed or behaves, public understanding can be distorted, and debates over wording can distract from the science.

The fight over what to call this object mirrors earlier classification battles, including Pluto's change to a dwarf planet. Definitions in astronomy are practical tools, not eternal truths: they get revised whenever observations stop matching the categories.

If future telescopes find many objects in similar layered orbits, astronomers may create a new category rather than forcing everything into 'planet' or 'moon.' Young researchers may lead the effort to define the next generation of cosmic vocabulary.
